title: Bangladesh garment workers reject owners' first wage offer; board talks resume Tuesday
dek: Employers proposed a minimum above Tk 14,500 a month against the workers' demand of Tk 30,000, as weeks of strikes and factory closures weigh on the country's biggest export.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Factory owners in Bangladesh made their first offer on Monday for a new minimum wage for workers in the country's more than 4,000 garment factories, and the workers' side rejected it as far too low. The government's Minimum Wage Board adjourned after several hours of talks in Dhaka and was due to resume at 2 pm on Tuesday (1.30 pm IST).

The board's chairman, Judge Syed Azad Subhani, said the employers' figure was above Tk 14,500 a month but did not give the exact number. Workers want the monthly minimum raised to Tk 30,000 from Tk 12,500, the level set in 2023. "The factory owners' offer is too low, while they accuse us of making excessive demands," said Babul Akhter, the workers' representative on the board, according to reports. He said the exact offers were being kept confidential to avoid "tension and confusion" during the talks.

## What happened at the board

The meeting, the board's third, began at about 11.45 am at the Labour Building in Segunbagicha, reports said. The owners put forward their proposal after two rounds of revisions, one report said; another report, citing board and industry sources, put the figure at Tk 15,800, which the board has not confirmed. Both sides are to study each other's proposals before revising them.

The owners' representative, ABM Shamsuddin, said the workers' demands were unrealistic given the state of the industry, comparing it to "a sick duck" that cannot be expected to lay a golden egg every day, according to reports. The manufacturers' association BGMEA has estimated that the protests have cost the industry $428 million and that orders worth $254 million have moved to other countries, reports said; those figures come from the employers and have not been independently checked.

Outside, several hundred workers formed a human chain demanding higher pay and the reopening of shut factories. "Our demand is clear: the minimum wage for workers must be Tk 30,000. Otherwise, we will launch a bigger movement," Nazma Akter, president of the Sommilito Garments Sramik Federation, said in an interview.

## How we got here

The government reconstituted the wage board on 1 November amid protests that began in October. At its first meeting on 4 November the board agreed the new wage would take effect in December, and many workers went back to work. The workers' side then formally proposed Tk 32,000 for the main grade. When a meeting due on 16 November was postponed, unrest flared again in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj, with workers blocking the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, police using tear gas and sound grenades, and dozens of factories declaring holidays.

The gap is wide by past standards. In 2023, workers asked for about Tk 20,000 to 23,000 and settled for Tk 12,500 after the owners raised their first offer of Tk 10,400; four workers died in the protests that year, according to reports. In each of the past five wage boards, employers have opened at half or less of the workers' demand, one report said.

## Why it matters for India

Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, and garments bring in about four-fifths of its export earnings, roughly $38 billion a year. Indian textile and apparel exporters compete with Bangladeshi factories for many of the same European and American buyers, so the outcome of the dispute affects costs and orders on both sides of the border. Bengal, which shares more than 2,000 km of the border, also trades heavily with Bangladesh through land ports such as Petrapole.

The dispute also lands at a fragile moment in Dhaka, where the government has deployed Border Guard Bangladesh platoons in the capital and several districts amid political violence ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return. If Tuesday's talks fail, unions have threatened wider protests.
